red.focus: Separate association from cause in legal evidence
red.summary: Two things can move together without one producing the other. Learn to ask what else might explain an observed pattern before advising that a legal policy worked.
checklist: I can describe an association without claiming cause
I can identify a plausible confounder
I can ask what would happen without the policy

sections.title: A Pattern Is Not an Explanation
sections.body_md: A town adds street cameras, and reported theft declines. The events occur together, but the decrease could also reflect seasonal changes, new patrols or shifts in reporting. Correlation is a relationship between variables; causation means that changing one factor produces a change in another. A legal-economic analyst should distinguish the two before claiming the cameras justified a restriction on privacy. The observed pattern is evidence worth investigating, not a complete proof.

sections.title: Look for a Comparison
sections.body_md: To estimate a policy's effect, ask what would likely have happened without it. A similar town without cameras might provide a comparison, but only if important differences and concurrent changes are considered. The ideal counterfactual cannot be observed directly for the same place and time. The analyst therefore looks for credible evidence approximating it. This habit prevents legal advocacy from treating the policy's implementation date as the cause of every later improvement.

sections.title: Describe What the Data Actually Say
sections.body_md: A report should specify which crimes were counted, how they were recorded, when the policy began and whether other conditions changed. Without clear measures, even a strong trend may be misleading. The lawyer can use the evidence to question or support a proposal while acknowledging its limits. Honest causal language helps clients and lawmakers evaluate policy without granting a statistic more authority than it deserves.

yellow.focus: Use comparison groups to strengthen causal inference
yellow.summary: Learn why experiments and carefully constructed observational comparisons can be more informative than before-after changes alone. Recognize baseline differences and selection effects.
checklist: I can explain a treatment and comparison group
I can identify why random assignment helps
I can recognize remaining limitations of an experiment

sections.title: Compare With What Would Happen Otherwise
sections.body_md: A legal aid program begins in some districts but not others. Researchers compare dispute outcomes between participating and nonparticipating places. That comparison may reveal an effect if the groups are otherwise sufficiently comparable. Random assignment, when lawful and ethical, can reduce systematic differences on average. But it does not guarantee perfect measurement, no attrition or applicability to every other jurisdiction. A good causal claim explains the comparison and its limitations.

sections.title: Selection Can Mislead
sections.body_md: Suppose only highly motivated applicants enroll in a voluntary legal training course. Their later success might reflect prior motivation as well as the training. Comparing participants with nonparticipants without addressing that difference can exaggerate the program's effect. Researchers may use baseline information, statistical methods or a better design, but each approach depends on assumptions. The analyst should ask how people entered the program and which variables could affect both participation and outcomes.

sections.title: Statistical Significance Is Not Impact
sections.body_md: A large study may detect a tiny change with high statistical confidence, while a smaller study may be inconclusive despite a potentially meaningful effect. Courts and policymakers should care about the size, uncertainty and practical consequences of an estimate, not only a threshold label. The law's normative question remains separate: does the measured effect justify the chosen intervention under applicable rights and authority? Evidence helps answer a part of that question, not all of it.

orange.focus: Assess quasi-experiments in legal policy evaluation
orange.summary: Public interventions often cannot be randomized. Learn the logic and assumptions of difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity and instrumental-variable approaches without treating them as magic proofs.
checklist: I can state the parallel-trends assumption
I can identify a plausible threshold design
I can explain why instruments require exclusion assumptions

sections.title: Difference-in-Differences
sections.body_md: Suppose one state changes its wage law while a comparable state does not. Difference-in-differences compares how outcomes change in each place, subtracting the control trend from the treated trend. Its causal interpretation often relies on a parallel-trends assumption: absent treatment, their outcomes would have evolved similarly. If one state also experiences an economic shock, the assumption may fail. A useful analysis plots pre-policy trends and explains why the comparison is credible rather than trusting the method's name.

sections.title: Regression Discontinuity
sections.body_md: A benefit becomes available only when household income falls below a threshold. Researchers may compare cases just above and below that cutoff, where characteristics can be similar. The design requires assumptions about continuity and whether people can manipulate the assignment variable. It can estimate a local effect near the threshold, not necessarily the effect on every household. A lawyer reviewing such evidence should identify the relevant population and whether the result can justify the broader policy claim.

sections.title: Instrumental Variables
sections.body_md: A researcher may use a variable that changes exposure but is assumed not to influence the outcome except through that exposure. Such an instrument can help address confounding under demanding conditions, including relevance and exclusion. A seemingly clever instrument can fail if it affects outcomes through another route. The analyst must explain those assumptions in ordinary language and test their plausibility. Econometric terminology cannot replace the burden of making the causal reasoning intelligible.

black.focus: Critique causal identification and the ethics of legal experiments
black.summary: At doctoral depth, examine what can be learned from policy experiments when treatment changes institutions and people respond strategically. Evaluate spillovers, external validity and consent.
checklist: I can identify threats to internal and external validity
I can explain why spillovers complicate treatment comparisons
I can propose ethically defensible evaluation of high-stakes legal policies

sections.title: The Intervention Changes the World
sections.body_md: A new sentencing policy may alter prosecutor offers, police behavior and defendants' plea decisions. The 'treatment' is not just a number assigned by researchers; institutions and people adjust in response. Spillovers can affect comparison groups, and local estimates may not transport to other courts with different rules. A doctoral evaluator must define the estimand—the causal effect actually sought—and explain which assumptions permit inference. Otherwise an impressive regression may answer a different question from the legal one.

sections.title: Legal Experimentation Has Ethical Limits
sections.body_md: Randomizing access to life-preserving representation or essential benefits can raise ethical and legal concerns. Policy evaluation must respect consent, equality, lawful authority and independent oversight. Sometimes a natural experiment or phased rollout offers more acceptable evidence, though each has methodological limits. A rigorous design should explain why its information gains justify the burdens placed on participants. No desire for a clean causal estimate permits disregard of human rights.

sections.title: Replication and Policy Learning
sections.body_md: A single study may show an effect in one court, time or population. A policy claim becomes stronger when methods, data and results can be scrutinized and findings recur in relevant settings. Yet replication itself must respect confidentiality and data protection. A doctoral legal scholar should state the result's uncertainty, possible mechanisms and limits of transportability before recommending national reform. The goal is law that learns from evidence while remaining accountable to the people it governs.
